cells.tense: You're mid-course with your hands on it, adding and setting down as the thing in front of you asks.
cells.ask: Tell one person the shape of your last stretch — witness offered, not asked
cells.core:
You add when the piece needs adding and set down what's finished, and that sensing comes so steadily you stopped noticing yourself do it. Nothing is being forced from either end. Here is the plain picture of this going well: a kitchen where the pot gets stirred before it boils over and the empty pan goes in the sink without ceremony — small calls, made on time, no drama in the room.

Telling someone the shape of your last stretch teaches you, in one breath, where the balance actually sits — which parts took more than they showed, and which one you've been keeping to yourself. A stretch gets noticed once it's outside you.

cells.tense: You're already fielding what nobody has handed you yet, bracing for a version of this that hasn't started.
cells.ask: Finish one task through to its end before you start the next — stop it there
cells.core:
You're adjusting ahead of the thing itself — imagining which piece will fall over next, which need will become yours, what you'll have to patch before it ever splits. The sensing still runs, but it's running into a future that hasn't arrived, and the hands that do the actual work are the ones paying for it.

In good shape this is a bench where you pick up one thing, work it, set it down, and pick up the next when the last is actually finished — the timing of the room set by what's in front of you, not by what's coming. Doing one task fully and stopping there, watching it hold without you, teaches that finishing is allowed. Something as small as a shelf hung, a form sent, a call returned and not followed with another lets you find where completion actually stops, and what waiting feels like in your own body.

cells.tense: You used to handle this well, and something in you is still back at the last time it stopped working.
cells.ask: Put twenty minutes on a timer with what you've left undone and sit with it
cells.core:
The care didn't run out — the timing is what got stuck. You sense what something needs and don't get to the move, and it's been like that long enough that adding and setting down don't seem to land anymore. More effort poured in won't bring the balance back; pushing harder at a thing that's gone quiet only tires the hands.

When it's working well here, the picture is simple: something gets picked up, worked a little, put down again because it's done or because it's not today's — and nothing in the room is on fire. Twenty minutes beside what you've left undone teaches you whether you're finished with it or only avoiding it, and either answer is a place to work from. What you find is information, not a verdict, and it doesn't ask you to fix anything today.

cells.tense: The balance is already being managed — you're in it, adjusting the whole way through — and you're telling yourself it's running itself.
cells.ask: Say out loud, once, which part of this you've been the one keeping steady
cells.core:
You're the calibration. You notice when something needs a lighter hand, when it needs picking up again, when the mix is off, and you answer that without ever counting it as yours. When it's going well, this is a kitchen where you reach for the salt before anyone's said the soup is flat — the correction lands and then it's nobody's business, least of all yours.

Saying which piece you've been keeping steady does two things at once: the work gets the name it belongs to, and the effort stops being invisible. Said once, what's finished is allowed to be finished, and the one who did the work gets the easier breath that follows.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim in my draft was that the person has been 'carrying' specific unspoken parts or that a particular task will 'hold without you' — the record names care and form, not what those hands have actually done or who receives them, so I've kept every example as something generic the person can pick up or set down. A reader could reasonably say the Too Little cell assumes the care still exists when it may simply be finished, so the ask is framed as sitting with what's undone to find out, not as resuming anything. Each ask survives a wrong read: telling one person, finishing one thing and stopping, twenty minutes on a timer, one sentence out loud — each teaches something about timing or honesty even if the card is wrong. The sentence that served the writer most was the Too Much cell wanting to diagnose worry; it's rewritten as timing, which the card actually says.
